The particular individual to whom I . have already referred was here during the Liberal regime and interviewed the then Alinister of Labour on innumerable occasions. The same person has brought before me five delegations in regard to the matter, and she wants another interview next week. She wants special legislation to be brought down.

The minister
might as well be in the trenches.

Yes. I received from several boards of trade and other organizations-I do not remember any of those to which my hon. friend has referred letters formally endorsing the whole scheme. In several cases I wrote back asking where they had got the idea that I intended to introduce legislation, and they referred me to this one source. I believe every one of those signatures which my hon. friend has read 'has been secured in that way. We all understand that if a lady, especially if she is young and charming, comes and asks us, we would sign a petition of that kind at once. I believe that the'majority of those signatures are attributable to the charming influence she exerts, and I have no doubt that she has exerted it on my hon. friend-
I have not been so fortunate.
I have no doubt that the material which he has read to-day has been supplied by that individual.
You miss your guess.

I dare say that if I had had the pleasure of the acquaintance of this estimable young lady whom the minister . knows so well, and who calls on him so often, I would have made a much better presentation of the case which I am trying to lay before the committee than I have done. I am not, however, as fortunate as the Alinister of Labour in knowing the young lady. I am sorry to learn that the minister is not going to introduce this legislation this year. He says that he has no recollection of having given this interview to the Evening Journal, and he also says that the Evening Journal is a very reliable paper. As it is a very reliable paper and as this article contains almost every word regarding this bureau that the Minister of Labour has uttered here to-day, I would infer, since the minister says that he does not remember, that he must certainly have given this interview to the Evening Journal. Be that as it may, tnere is not much use in my discussing the question much further in view of the fact that it is not the intention of the Minister of Labour to introduce legislation at the present session for the establishment of a national labour bureau in Canada. Inis information will be received with deep regret by the people of this country. I hope the time will come when we shall have in this country a Minister of Labour who will take this question up with a more lively interest than* has been shown [by my hon. friend
49C

who now holds the position. I do not care whether he be a Conservative or a Liberal; I hope he will fill the need that we have had in this country for a long time.

Some of the representatives of the Trades and Labour Congress which met at St. John in September last were from my hon. friend's own town, and they voted in favour of the resolution to which I have referred.

I am willing to wager the hon. minister that there is not a member o,f the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress in the city of Sydney or in the town of Glace Bay who would not vote for the establishment of a national labour bureau in Canada.

The resolution was carried unanimously, and representatives from my hon. friend's town were there and I understood voted for the resolution, although I do not undertake to say definitely that such is the case.

I just want to suggest to the minister that either his department or the Immigration Department could do some good if they had a means of placing with the farmers men who have worked on farms. The spring is coming on and a great many men could be placed in the riding from which I come, and, I believe, in the riding from which the minister comes. There are a great many mechanics who are accustomed to farm labour.
Have you not in your town an agent appointed by the Immigration Department? -There is one at St. Thomas. [DOT]
There may be one, but I have not heard of him.
My hon. friend had better loolj him up and ask him for farm help.

Personally I have never had any difficulty in getting help. I have a number of applications for help at the present time, but there are a number of men in my section of the country who I know are willing to hire men now.
I am told by my deputy that these agents last year distributed amongst the farmers 20,000 men. That is the report from the Immigration office.

In the debate on the Address I asked whether or not the fair-wage clause had been put into force dn*con-
nection with the contracts let in Canada for the supply of various articles for war purposes, and I pointed out that, as there is an English fair-wage clause similar to the one we have in Canada, it was the duty of the Department of Labour, in letting these contracts, to see that this provision was carried out. I understand that representations were made to the department from my section, where some of the shells are being made. Has a fair-wage officer gone to New Glasgow or that vicinity, or has anything been done in the way of looking into and adjusting this matter in regard to not merely to wages, but to the working hours of the men employed in some of these industries?
The same company is running a plant at Amherst, is it not?
No, a different company. You might tell us also about the company at Amherst.

There are about a hundred factories in Canada making bodies for shells for the British Government. Our fair-wage clause does not apply to any of these contracts.
I think the right hon. Prime Minister, in answering a question put by my hon. friend a few days ago, told him that these contracts are being let by a board appointed by the Minister of Militia, the chairman of which is Colonel Bertram, of Montreal. We received complaints from three different places to the effect that fair wages were not * being paid and that the men were obliged to work long hours. We replied at once saying that we had not the power to enforce any fair-wage clause, but that we would take the matter up with the chairman of that board, Colonel Bertram. That gentleman has taken a great interest in this matter, and has a very strong sympathy for the working people, mechanics in particular. He went to Toronto to go into the factories the men working in which were strongest in their complaints; he also went into those in the Montreal district. He said that he entirely sympathized with the complaints made by these men; that the manufacturers of these bodies were receiving fair profit and there was no reason why they should not pay the men fair wages. He said he would see to it that fair-wage clauses were put in future contracts, and that no contract would be awarded unless this grievance was at once remedied. The superintendent of one of the Toronto companies came here; I saw him, and he understood before he left that he would have to deal fairly with the men;

otherwise he would make no more shells.
I understand that he has proceeded to put things in proper shape so far as the men are concerned. I find Colonel Bertram exceedingly anxious to do everything he can to adjust matters in this respect. The complaint that came from the firm to which my hon. friend refers was handed over to Colonel Bertram. He is a very busy man, but I have no doubt he will see to it that the men in my hon. friend's constituency will get a fair deal.

I agree with what
the hon. minister says respecting Colonel Bertram; I know him personally and regard him as a very high-class man. While the situation may be remedied temporarily in some quarters, I think the minister ought in some way to assert control over his fair-wage officers in regard to these matters. I do not think that the minister, simply because Colonel Bertram says he will look into the matter, should refrain from any further attempt to have his fair-wage officers take action.

I neglected to tell my hon. friend that I sent officers to London, Toronto and Hamilton. They went into the factories, and I have full reports from them. I should be glad, however, if my hon. friend would suggest anything that I can do, apart from Col. Bertram, to remedy these grievances.

In England they have a fair-wage provision for Government contracts, just as we have in Canada. These contracts for supplies are important contracts, let through a committee appointed by the Government of Canada, so that although the money is not paid directly by the Government of Canada, it is paid through a body created for the purpose of carrying out the wishes of the Imperial Government. While it is well that Col. Bertram should undertake to look into these matters, I think the minister ought to send his fair-wage officers into localities from which complaints may come, in order to ascertain the nature of the grievances existing with respect to wages and labour. I am referring particularly to a communication which I understand was sent to the Minister of Labour from New Glasgow on behalf of a large number of men who are employed there, asking that a fair-wage officer be sent to that district. The minister has intimated that he sent men to Lon-
5 p.m. don and elsewhere, and if he has not already sent one to Nova Scotia, I would ask him to do so in order that the necessary inquiries may be made.

I may say further that we had communication on this subject with the British War Office, through Sir George Perley, and the British War Office said in substance that they did not want the men in Canada to work under anything but fair conditions. My deputy informs me that a copy of the correspondence touching that matter was sent to Col. Bertram. It is not always practicable to send a fair-wage officer unless definite complaints are received.
I understood that my hon. friend had received a letter from the labour people of that district.

Yes, and the letter
was referred to Colonel Bertram. In many cases we sent men to districts thousands of miles distant to investigate complaints of a general character, with the result that no real grievance was found to exist. Consequently we insist upon receiving definite particulars with regard to wages, hours of labour, etc. I think we have done everything we can do in the matter. Colonel Bertram and his colleagues act, in a sense, under our authority through the Minister of Militia. I am satisfied with what he is doing, and I am glad my hon. friend knows him and corroborates what I have said in regard to his activities. I believe that he is very much in earnest about this matter, and that he will remedy conditions so far as it is possible to do so, even going to the extent of withholding further contracts if necessary.
Who is the fair-wage officer supervising these matters in the maritime provinces.

Mr. Dubreuil. My
deputy informs me that the communication received from New Glasgow referred to ^ome condition that might be brought about, not to anything at present existing.

Has the minister's attention been called to a letter sent to his department in November last from the International Brotherhood of Steam Shovel and Dredge Men at Thorold, in the county of Welland? I have a copy of a letter, which is addressed to the Department of Labour, Ottawa, from this body, pointing out the minimum and maximum scale of wages paid to that class of men. The suggestion is made that something be done in the direction of fixing a definite scale of wages for these men, not only on regular days but on holidays and for overtime as well. Has anything been done?

As my hon. friend is aware, five different contractors are working on the Welland canal. I think that during the last eight or ten months, one of our fair wage officers has been there practically half the time. I do not remember having seen the complaint my hon. friend refers to.
This is not really in the nature of a complaint; it is suggesting what should be done by the department.
Do you think that letter indicates that there is no schedule of wages?

I understand that there
is not a schedule, and they want one fixed.

The matter has not
been brought to my attention before, but I will look into it. I understand that there is a fixed schedule for all classes of labour employed on the canal.
If my hon. friend has not seen this letter, I will hand it to him so that he can look over it.

All right. We insist on the contractors adhering strictly to the schedules, and we have succeeded in getting large sums of money for men who have worked on the canal in different capacities. But it is a herculean task to keep track of it. I shall be very glad to look into this matter.

The minister has referred to what the Government of Alberta is doing in the way of assisting the unemployed in some of the cities of that province. We can understand the cause of a good deal of the unemployment that exists; but there is a peculiar class of unemployment in a certain section of my constituency. I have taken this matter up with the minister by correspondence* and in interviews, and I wish to deal with it on the floor of the House merely to bring about if possible an effort on the part of the Government to look into this particular condition. The coal mines on the prairies of Alberta have been practically without work all this winter. I should, however, except the Galt mine in the city of Lethbridge. The Galt mine is the oldest domestic coal mine in Southern Alberta. It has an established market as far east as the city of Winnipeg, and on that account has been able to keep up a good business. But the other mines adjacent to Lethbridge have been working less than half time. East of there is the mining camp of Taber

a very extensive camp. I would say that there are eight to ten coal mines, large and small. I have satisfied myself that the mines of Taber from the beginning of 1914 up to the present time have not furnished work to the miners in that camp to the extent of a day and a half a week. That information wras given to me, and I have investigated it and found it to be corroborated by the statements of others. There must be some reason for this condition. We may have a period of depression in the country during which we may do without certain things; but there is one thing the people of western Canada cannot do without, and that is fuel. The winter in Southern Alberta this year commenced the latter part of November and has continued up to the present time, and it was not the open winter we usually have in that part of the country, but a real winter which made fuel absolutely necessary. No doubt economy has been practised; people may have used less coal than they did in other years. There has also been a development of the natural gas area and in a great many communities in Alberta natural gas has supplanted coal as a fuel. But I cannot believe that it is for these reasons that the time of the workingmen at Taber camp has been reduced on an average to a day and a half a week during the year. I have mentioned to the minister the establishment of a new and extensive camp at Drumheller, northwest of Calgary, and there is no question that it has been cutting into the business of the Southern Alberta mines in Central Saskatchewan and Central Alberta. But the condition at Taber is an economic matter to a large extent, [DOT]and I think requires an investigation. Charges have been made that some of the transportation companies are not assisting the mines at Taber, that they are operating against them, that in bringing back their empties this year the railways have filled them with a good deal of coal from the East which has come into competition with Western Canada coal. I do not know whether that is correct. But I know that in the camp at Taber the miners have been practically without work for a year, that there has been a great deal of distress and poverty, that there is no hope of employment ahead or that the situation will brighten. I think this matter is worthy of * the attention of the Department of Labour, and that an investigation should be made by some person who is acquainted with mining, and who will be impartial in his investigation. I have had in mind that it

might be possible for even the Railway Commission to look into this matter of alleged discrimination, and ascertain whether there is any truth in the charges. The prevailing opinion among the miners in that district is that the railways are discriminating against them.
I will anticipate a question that might be asked. It might be stated that the duty on coal should be increased; that American coal is supplanting our Alberta coal. I take no stock in that argument, because the duty has not been changed, except at the present session, and American coal has always had the same opportunity to come into western Canada as at present, and in past years this condition did not exist in the Taber and other western camps. Again there has been no labour trouble in the mining camps of Alberta during the past year. Things have been running smoothly between the union and the operators, due largely to the fact that there was not very much work for the men to do and it was not to their advantage to have any difficulty with the operators.
They have been quiet for three years.

The situation, nevertheless, is very severe, and I am bringing it to the attention of the House with the hope that an effort will be made by the Government to bring about a solution of the situation particularly at Taber. My opinion is that there is something economically wrong; for they had a market before, but-now for two winters conditions have been extremely bad, and there is no improvement in site. I think it is worth while for the country to investigate this charge of discrimination on the part of the railways, and if discrimination is found to exist to remove it if possible. I know that officials of the Labour Department have looked into conditions at Taber camp. 1 believe that if the minister paid a visit to Taber and saw the conditions there he would appreciate the need of some immediate actidh.

I regret very much that there has been so little work at Taber for so many months. Early in the fall I sent a fair wage officer from Vancouver to inquire into conditions there and later I wrote to my hon. friend (Mr. Buchanan) about it. He was kind enough to answer my letter and to give me all the information he had at his disposal. I have talked the matter over with him since the beginning of the session. Neither he nor I so far have been
able to devise any means for relieving the situation there. He mentioned that perhaps the principal cause of the difficulty at Taber was the opening of another mine at Drum-heller where they can get coal and supply the wants of many people in the province with a shorter haul than if they were to take it from Taber. I do not know that any one is to blame for that. I suppose that if a man buying coal finds he can get it at Drum-heller cheaper than he can at Taber he will get it at Drumheller and that will lessen the work for the miners at Taber. I am told that the coal produced at Taber is not of as good quality as that produced in some other parts of the province and that is given as a reason why coal is imported and brought from Other places. I understand that the Canadian Pacific railway is interested in the mines at Lethbridge, which my hon. friend has referred to, and that the miners are very busy there. The miners at Taber wrote me asking me to make a personal visit to Taber and my hon. friend desired me to do that too. Taber is in his constituency and if he will give me the assurance from his experience of the people there that if I go everything will be all right, I will make an extra effort to go.

Do you think you
can do that?

My hon. friend (Mr. Buchanan) succeeds with the people at Taber and suggests that I should go. I do not claim to know anything about mining, but I will speak to the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and also to my colleagues and see if it would be possible to have the matter investigated by the Board. I cannot understand what good I could do these people by going out there personally, although they insist on my going.
They would like to see you.
If that would please them and settle the difficulty I would be delighted to go, but I do not see wherein I could do very much more for them personally. It may be that an investigation will be held.

This is what is called domestic coal. With regard to the steam coal mines in the Crowsnest pass, there might be some reason for the slackness of work on account of the fact that the railways are not operating as they formerly were and some other industries are closed down and

therefore are not using as much coal. Domestic coal ought to be in general use from year to year.

I know that in certain sections of the West they much prefer Galt coal, and that they do not buy Taber coal if they can get the other. They are willing to pay as much as fifty cents extra for the Galt coal in preference to the Taber coal. I presume it is fairly good coal, but the Galt coal is preferred.

With regard to the question of coal in the west, coming as I do from a coal section in the East, the information I have about, the situation there -and the figures verify it-is that during the last two or three years there has been a tremendous displacement of coal in the western field, more in British Columbia than in Alberta, by reason of the fact that the \ise of fuel oil on locomotives on the different railways there has greatly increased. This would have its resultant effect upon domestic coal. I fancy the characteristics of the two kinds of coal are not defined in such a marked way that parties who produce coal, which they sold to the railways, would not, when they were driven from the railway supply; naturally seek a market in a great many places where the people who had been purchasing domestic coal, such as Taber coal, which people would be looked upon as affording a natural market for this domestic coal. There have been complaints coming from those who have gone from the East to the West as to the conditions which exist in a business way there, which conditions, of course, affect labour and these conditions are no doubt largely due to the tremendous importation of fuel oil displacing coal in the business of the country. I mention this as being one of the causes which the minister will have to consider in regard to the request made by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan), because I have no doubt that he has had the same problem submitted to him from the coal people on the other side of the mountain.
How many labour disputes have been settled through the intervention of the minister's department during the past year?

At the time of the outbreak of the war I publicly requested all employers and employees to avoid as far as possible any labour disturbances pointing out that we required our united strength

to fight the enemy and that it would be unwise to dissipate that in any way by disputes between employers and employees. There were two or three disputes at that time approaching the appointment of a board of conciliation, but I was very much pleased to find that employers and employees got together and settled their trouble as I had suggested. We have not had a board of conciliation since although I think there are three at Edmonton in process of formation now. They are not large questions and I am in hopes that they will be able to settle them so that they may not require a board at all. Apart from that there have been about eighteen boards of conciliation during the past year. We have not had any serious trouble with any matter that has been dealt with under the Industrial Disputes Act.
Were the 17 or 18 boards that were appointed successful in bringing disputes to a satisfactory termination?

I think they succeeded.
I think both parties, with one or two slight exceptions, accepted the awards made by the board.

The Act appears to be working pretty well for both parties concerned. Is it the intention of the minister to bring in any amendment, or has he been asked by any parties or organizations, to prepare a Bill in amendment of the existin'* Act?	6

Yes, I have been asked, and I have prepared a Bill, but it would be unwise to bring it up at this time. Some suggestions I have to make would not meet the wishes of all classes of working people, and as there would be a controversy no doubt I have determined not to bring that legislation in this year. Speaking generally, I want to testify to the fairly satisfactory working of the Industrial Disputes Act, so far as my experience goes. As no doubt my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) knows, his native province is entitled to the credit for the main features of the Industrial Disputes Act. Credit is sometimes given to other places, but it was the legislature of Nova Scotia that, in the year 1890, adopted the chief features of that legislation. I think the Industrial Disputes Act operates fairly well.
I desire to make some improvements to it and then I believe it will be as satisfactory as any similar legislation in any part of the world.
Has the commission on the high cost of living made a report?

They promised me a couple of weeks ago that their report would be ready before the end of the month. I think it is about ready now, and I think my hon. friend and other hon. gentlemen will find it a very able report and a very satisfactory one, especially the work in connection with it which was done in my department, and of which I am very proud.

The question of
technical education is, of course, a very large one, and in our province, in which we have a very large industrial population developing our various resources, there is a very satisfactory technical school, which has been started by the Provincial Government. The results so far produced by that school have been of such beneficial character that we all have become greatly interested in the subject and we look forward to the extension of technical schools with a good deal of hope. There are four or five constituencies in Nova Scotia which seem to have led the way, so far as the country east of Quebec is concerned, in industrial development. Nova Scotia was the scene of the inception of the iron and steel industries of the Dominion, the initiation and progress of which have been due entirely to latent Nova Scotian talent. The Nova Scotia Government has established a technical school under the direction of Professor Sexton.

One of the best in
Canada.

One of the best in
Canada, and the beneficial results obtained from that school have attracted the attention of our people. One does not need to elaborate upon the desirability of extending the operation of the technical schools system among the working people of Canada. The report of the Commission on Technical Education has been before the minister for some time, and I would like to have him make a frank statement as to what his views in regard to that question are, and what his idea is at to what can be done in the future.

When the Commission on Technical Education was appointed, the question of jurisdiction as between the Dominion and the provinces was raised, and so that there might be no misunderstanding the Prime Ministers of the various provinces were told that the object of this commission would be only to collect information and report that information to the various provincial governments. They were asked whether they in any way objected to
the appointment of such commission. The Prime Ministers of all the provinces replied, saying that they had no objection, but Prime Ministers of Quebec and Ontario drew special attention to the fact that under the British North America Act education was within the purview of the provinces. The report was completed in February last, and on the 12th of March it was sent to the Prime Minister of each province with the accompanying letter:
Ottawa, March 12, 1914.
My Dear Sir,-You will, perhaps, recall communications exchanged in December, 1909, between my predecessor as Minister of Labour and yourself, with reference to the advisability of the appointment by the Dominion Government of a Royal Commission " to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects industrial training and technical education," etc., my predecessor going on to remark, " It is intended that the commission shall be solely for the purpose of gathering information, the information, when obtained, to be published in a suitable report to be at the disposal of the provinces and available for general distribution." Letters were similarly exchanged on this subject with the Prime Ministers of the other provinces of Canada. None of the replies received objected to the appointment of the commission, and several contained expressions of cordial approval of the proposed course of action.
The Dominion Government appointed a Royal Commission in June, 1910, and the commission in clue course reported. I deemed it well, before bringing the report formally ta your attention, to await receipt of the concluding section (Part IV), in view particularly of the fact that this part contains a report of the inquiry of the commission in Canada itself. Copies of this part having been received, the four volumes comprising the report are now sent you, and I should be pleased to receive, as soon as may be possible, an expression of your views as to the general nature of the report, and especially concerning the recommendations contained therein. Any suggestion you may be pleased to make will be submitted to my colleagues, and will receive, you may rest assured, careful consideration.
The earlier volumes of the report have been already forwarded to each member of your Government and to many of your leading officers.
Yours faithfully,
JJ\ W. Crothers.
I received a reply from all of the prime ministers, acknowledging the receipt of this report, but there was no indication that the Provincial Governments would take the matter up seriously, nor did they make any suggestions as to whether they were in favour of the report of the commission or not. The communication from Premier Murray, of Nova Scotia, was an exception, in that as he takes a special interest in the subject, he did go more fully into the question than did the others. The question

My hon. friend has not indicated what his aspirations are in regard to this matter, but has confined himself to the simple statement that on account of the financial condition of the country he is unable to propose anything at all.
Mr. CROTHERcS: My hon. friend will remember that I did not confine myself to that one point.

Beyond showing a pious sympathy, my hon. friend intimated that, as there was no money at hand to spend, he would not say what should be done. My hon. friend ought to take the initiative. I have no doubt the Premier of Nova Scotia has suggested to him that he should follow the line adopted by the hon. Minister of Agriculture in connection with the special vote made for the purpose of assisting agriculture in this country. When I say that I do not know what the Hon. Mr. Murray has said, I am only supposing that he may have suggested this course to the Minister of Labour. Where in any province of the Dominion there is a well-established technical school, it would <b' desirable to

supplement and extend its operations by assistance from the federal treasury along the same lines as assistance was granted to agriculture. The minister should not wait for the provincial ministers to tell him what he should do on this question. That is where I find fault with him. We admit that the financial condition of the country to-day is such that the Minister of Finance has to be very cautious when his brother ministers come to him with proposals involving inroads upon the treasury. We all know that he is bound to exercise the strictest economy in every quarter in order to maintain the financial status of Canada. He would be liable to criticism if he failed to take that position. I am sure that we on this side of the House will support him in that wise and cautious policy, if he follows it, endeavouring to keep things on an even keel. But assuming that he does so and that our business is to continue this war until it is brought to a successful conclusion, that ought not to prevent the Minister of Labour from having upon this question some policy, some views, which he may desire to carry into effect when the smoke of battle has cleared away and the Empire is sailing upon a level sea and Canada is following her usual course. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour apparently has no views on this question at all. Because the premiers of the different provinces have not suggested to him what he should do, he does not do anything and does not even propose to think about the matter. I entreat my hon. friend to get into a different frame of mind upon this question. Not only do we want to see this country great agriculturally, but where we have the facilities and the natural resources we want to see it great industrially. We cannot see it great industrially, unless we lay the foundation for that condition by a system of technical education. One of the things that has made Germany such a wonderful nation as she is in the way of providing modern devices relating to war, has been her system of technical education, which she has pursued with the greatest care for the last 20 or 25 years. In this new country of ours, where we are but laying the foundations, we should, at the earliest possible date, not merely provincially but federally, deal with this problem, so that we may lay a permanent basis of conditions upon which Canada may build an industrial structure which will give her a foremost place among the new nations of

the world. I beseech my hon. friend to adopt some policy upon this question; for apparently he has not any policy. I would like to know what he would do if he had the money. If he will frame a policy I am sure the people of Canada will supply the necessary money when the skies are clear.

This matter of technical education is very important in the province of Nova Scotia. Has there been under the advisement of the Department of Labour or of the Government any scheme whereby the provinces might be assisted in the matter of technical education along the lines of the report of the commission appointed for that purpose?

The matter has been
under consideration along the lines suggested by the members of the commission as well as along some other lines. Some of the provinces do not agree at all with the suggestions made by the commissioners. The report comprises four large volumes, which were sent out only last March. It would take a man a long time to read them, and a longer time to consider them. It is the intention of the Government, when the skies are clear, as my hon. friend the member for Pictou says, if we can make saisfactory arrangements with the provinces, to render material assistance in respect to technical education.
Conciliation and Labour Act, including publication, printing, binding and distribution of the Labour Gazette, and allowance to correspondents and for clerical assistance in preparing tables on statistics, $35,000.
What is the situation in regard to the British Columbia labour question?

A short time ago I
asked my fair wage officer at Vancouver to go over to Vancouver Island and give me a detailed report as to conditions of mines there, and he did so, giving the number of white people and the number of Orientals working in each mine. What my hon. friend no doubt refers to particularly is the labour trouble which has existed on Vancouver Island for a long time. The strike was called off some months ago and a great many of the men have returned to work, and some of them have moved out, but everything is quiet there now.

A recent issue of the
Labour Gazette reported that the United Mine Workers paid out a million and a half dollars of their funds in conducting that strike. Is that correct?
I understand that that is about the amount they paid out.

An article in a recent
issue of the Labour Gazette, dealing with coal mining and, I think, not contributed by the regular correspondent, contained a statement which would lead people to believe that Sydney is a coal mining city. There is not a coal mining town within ten miles of the city of Sydney. The town of Glace Bay is the centre of the coal mining operations, and Sydney is the centre of the steel industry. The matter was brought to my attention by a gentleman who thinks that the article is unfair to the city of Sydney; I merely call the minister's attention to it.

The correspondent of
the Labour Gazette in that district, Mr. John Moffat, is one of the best men we have in Canada.
This article was not contributed by the correspondent.
It was not contributed by Mr. Moffatt, but I fancy the editor based his article on information obtained from him. However, I shall look into the matter and see that it is remedied.
The correspondent in my county, Mr. Mackenzie, has gone to the war. Who is performing his duties during his absence?

We have had several cases of that kind. During the absence of the correspondent we pay him his salary, and pay a man to take his place, on the understanding that wnen the regular correspondent returns, he will resume his position.
Who is substituting in this case?
I do not remember the name; I will let my hon. friend know.

As my hon. friend
is aware, the coal situation in Eastern Canada is in a very bad way. Has the hon. member had any representations from' that section of the country with reference to slackness of work or other difficulties of a like nature?

I think we have had no complaints of that kind from the eastern provinces.

We reduced that vote by $5,000, as we did not expect as many



boards of conciliation this year as we had last year.
Mr- COPP: Has the minister received a resolution passed by the Moncton Trades and Labour Council with regard, to the payment of wages bi-monthly instead of monthly?
I think I did receive a communication of that kind.
Has the minister received a action in the matter?

This matter would
more properly come within the scope of the Department of Railways. It has been proposed that there should be an amendment to the Railways Act requiring all railway companies to pay wages twice instead of once a month. I myself suggested an amendment of that kind last year; when the Railway Act is revised I have no doubt that that matter will be discussed.

It seems to me that this is a matter which concerns more particularly the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Moncton than the different Railway unions. By these resolutions they have sought the good offices of the Minister of Labour; they believe that he is a friend of labour, I suppose, and hope that he will work out these matters in their interest. I should like to iknow from the minister whether he has taken any action in the matter, so that I may be in a position to advise those who have communicated with me in that regard.

I acknowledged receipt of the communication and promised, I think, to give the matter my favourable consideration and to consult the Minister of Railways about it. I have spoken -to the Minister of Railways; I do not know what will be done.

I fancy this refers to the Board of Conciliation which dealt with a dispute between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and their machinists at Winnipeg. A board was appointed in connection with this matter before I took charge of the Department of Labour, and an award was made. The Industrial Disputes Act provides that there shall be a board of investigation before there is a strike or lockout, and once the board has sat, heard evidence and made an award, any party to the dispute is at liberty to strike or to lockout, as they may see fit; there is no law against it. In the case to which, no doubt, they have reference, the machinists went on strike before the board sat; that was prior to October, 1911. An award was afterwards made and the company refused to carry that award out. An arrangement was made about a year and a half afterwards between the men and the company whereby the men were to go back and receive certain wages. Most of them went back to work at Trans-cona, near Winnipeg. The men contended that the company had not, as agreed, asked for a board, so they themselves asked for one. That was in the fall of 1913. Another board was appointed and another award made in favour of the men, which the company refused to recognize, contending that

the men had agreed that when they returned to work they would not ask for a board unless a majority of the employees in certain crafts were dissatisfied. The question at once arose whether there was a majority dissatisfied or a majority satisfied. The company said the majority of the men were satisfied; the men said that the majority were dissatisfied. The award of the board, however, was in favour of the men, and the company steadfastly refused to carry it out. The men have since continued to work.

They also thought it was not well to enact that they

could renew the lease from time to time; therefore, the Committee has amended the Bill so as to compel them to coine forward every time they desire to renew the lease and ask for a special sanction as a safeguard to the public interest.

The effect of the
legislation is to divest a Canadian company of control over the railway and to put the railway under the control of an American company.
To a certain extent. It is like the Michigan Central and Canada Southern.

To what extent has the committee reserved control over the New York Central operating this railway in Canada under our statutes. Does the chairman think that our laws are fully operative as against a foreign corporation?

Yes, under the Railway Aot the operating company is under the control of the railway commission. The New York Central becomes the operating company. Labour-Industrial Disputes Investigation , Act, $20,000.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to take up much of the time of the Committee but it seems to me that in my capacity of mayor of Montreal, it is incumbent on me to criticise the Government and specially the honourable Minister of Labour for neglecting to provide in the estimates an item of a few million dollars towards assisting the unemployed in the great industrial centres.
Of course, we were called upon to vote $150,000,000 to be spent in Great Britain for war purposes; but no provision whatever was made towards helping the workingman in the manufacturing centres of the Dominion. We have reached such a stage of misery that unless the Government realize what is going on and try to remedy matters, large numbers of our fellow-people are bound to starve.
In Montreal there are 45,000 of our people unemployed. The same state of things exists in all large cities of Ontario, and particularly Toronto. I deeply regret that this Government, and specially the Minister of Labour, should have overlooked the desirability of taking a vote towards helping out the destitute during this period of stress.
This morning, more than 800 unemployed called at my office at the City Hall; they included men in all class of society, accountants and clerks as well as laborers; for all our factories have closed down.
Therefore, I say that this Government should have been content with asking for a somewhat smaller amount to be forwarded to Great Britain. We are bound to borrow $150,000,000, that will be handed over to England; that money will not even cross the Atlantic, though we will have to pay interest on the loan and make good for it later on. We are willing to send men over there, but we should not send money, and I regret that no provision has been made for the destitute in this country, while millions are being sent to England.
Unless the Government make haste to assist our destitute, wa shall presently be threatened with a revolution. I say then that we should at once provide in the Estimates, either of the Public Works or of the Labour Department, an amount
sufficient to give work to our unemployed. Why not start forthwith the building of the Georgian Bay Canal? Why not carry out immediately the great work of improvement of the Montreal Harbour?
Times are hard, but the worst is yet to come.
The Minister of Labour need not laugh. It is a time to cry, not to laugh. It is very funny to see the Minister of Labour laughing when we are discussing questions of importance.
You did not see him laughing at all. You are making that up.
You were laughing. It is not a time to laugh.
I was not laughing.

I know you always laugh when you see citizens without bread in their house; but you will see, when the next election comes, that the shame will be on you.
* (Translation) Mr. Chairman, I say that the Minister of Labour has been remiss in his duty in neglecting to provide in his Estimates an amount sufficient to assist urban municipalities. Rural municipalities, whose inhabitants undergo no hardship and are in a position to sell their produce at a large profit, need no help on our part. In cities, however, conditions are vastly different from those existing in the country, workingmen cannot find employment and charitable associations, among them St. Vincent de - Paul find themselves unable to Gope with the numerous demands made upon resources.
The city of Montreal has provided $75,000 to supply bread and soup to these unfortunate people. In my view, municipalities are not alone responsible for the maintenance of these dependents. I think the Minister of Labour should pay a visit to the poorer sections of our city, that might induce him to alter his views.
They should change the mayor.

I think
rather we should change the government. At all events, I challenge the honourable member for l'Islet (Mr. Paquet) to try and have the people of Montreal change their mayor.

My hon. friend will recollect that the Commission of Technical Education was launched from the Labour Department. Its report was completed only last February. Had my hon. friend been in his place before six o'clock he would have heard a letter read that I sent to the Prime Ministers of the various provinces with this report requesting that they should give expression to their views as to its contents and recommendations. We may have inquiries made, or may have inquiries to make, and we put in this small sum to meet any expenses that may arise in connection with this matter.
You have not taken any action on the Commission's report?

The commission was appointed only to collect information and submit it to the various provinces, and this we have done. It does not follow that we are not to do any more. As my hon. friend knows, the subject of education is, according to the British North America Act, entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Unless some arrangement can be made with the provinces such as was made by the Minister of Agriculture in the matter of assisting agriculture, there will be nothing done. The commission recommended, as my hon. friend knows, that we should supply the provinces with $3,500,000 a year. But we thought that other matters were more immediately pressing and made a first demand upon the treasury and that we were not justified in making such an expenditure now.
Labour-Inspection of railway construction, etc., $10,000.
How is this money to be expended?

Up to a few years ago the Labour Department did not undertake to uo any work of this kind; but complaints came to us from the construction camps on the Grand Trunk Pacific and other railways 
that sanitary and hospital provisions were not being carefully looked after. We undertook an inspection. One of the fair-wage officers of my department made two trips from Edmonton to Prince Rupert. On the first trip, he found things in a horrible condition. By reason of his inspection and the action he took on it the principal complaints were remedied within two or three weeks after his report was made. He has been over that whole line a second time. We have inspected the construction camps on the other railways of Canada, and we expect to expend this sum, or a portion of it in the same way. We cannot know in advance how much we shall be required to spend. That will depend on the complaints that come in.
Who are the people employed in this work?

I understand that the
fair-wage officers are employed to go round the various public works to see that fair wages are being paid.

That is part of their
work. The principal work they did originally was to fix fair wages, according to thj current rates being paid in the district, on ally public work that might be going on. If a public building, for instance, is to be put up by the Public Works Department, they send a request for us to make a schedule giving minimum rates of wages that should be paid to the various trades, such as stone-cutters, bricklayers, carpenters and plumbers, that are to be engaged in the construction. One of the fair-wage officers goes to the district where the work is to be carried on and ascertains what the current rate of wages is and what are the hours of labour for similar work in that district. He then makes a report. Those who are to tender on the job see exactly' what they will have to pay the different craftsmen in the execution of their work. These officers do not go about inspecting these works unless complaint is made. But if complaint is made, for instance, against a contractor on the Welland canal or the contractors for public buildings, that they are not paying the wages, the fair-wage officer is sent to inquire into the circumstances and report, and we here try to see to it that the contractor pays what he should pay under the schedules contained

in the contract. These officers are sent out when a labour dispute arises even between two individuals. They are looking into the wages paid in the manufacture of shells now being supplied to the British Government. Anything of the nature of a dispute between employer and employed of either a private or a public character is investigated by one of these fair-wage officers.

I was amazed when a messenger brought into my office this morning copies of the Auditor General's Report. There were three volumes in English for 1914, but only one volume in French, and that was for 1913. As the minister is asking for a translator, I think he might explain why only one volume for 1913 is out.

That would concern the general staff of blue-book translators. I regret I have not with me Mr. Desaulniers' report, but if I remember rightly the translating staff lost four of its members by death last year, and their places were not filled for months and months. When these new men have had a little experience, things will get in better shape, and no doubt they will catch up with the work. When Mr. Desaulniers took charge of the translating staff, there was a great deal of work on hand to be done, and that accounts for the delay in getting out the French reports.
Will the minister have the translation done in his own department?

In the past the translation has been done outside, but it is our intention to have a translator in the department to translate purely departmental affairs. The blue-books of course are translated by the blue-book translation staff.

The practice of the departments varies. I understand that there is a translator in the Department of Agriculture, in the Post Office Department, and in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Only last week we appointed four translators for what is called the House branch. Personally, I think the proper w'ay is to have the translation done in the department. From what I have said about the Auditor General's Report the House will see under what a serious disadvantage the French population labours. Only one volume of the Auditor General's Report for 1913 has yet appeared in French, and yet we have translators for Hansard, translators for the Law Branch, translators for the House, and translators in the various departments. At present we have on the pay-list about 50 translators, whose salaries range from $1,500 to $2,000. We probably spend about $100,000 on translation alone. My hon. friend will

see how useless it would be to send out one volume of the Auditor General's Report for 1913 in French, when he could send the whole report for 1914 in English. I think the minister is taking the proper step in appointing a translator to his own department. I must congratulate the Postmaster General upon the fact that the French report of his department was out ten days after the English report was published. There is some sense in that. The Marine Department, although short in one section, if I remember correctly, was only a few months behind with its French report. I do not know who is to blame for the delay in translating the Auditor General's Report. The correspondence at the beginning is the only thing that would have to be translated, for the rest is made up of names and figures. But certainly there has been omission somewhere. could go ahead with the manuscript, whereas when the translators are clubbed together they have to wait for the whole bound volume before they can start work, and they are bound to be behind time.

the intention of the Government when they appointed translators to have one in each department translating blue-books. I understand that that is the work of the blue-book translation staff. There is an increased expenditure in this department and we should not allow the vote to pass without recording our protest. Notwithstanding the falling off in business there seems to be no attempt made at economy in this department, although some of the other departments have made a pretence at it. At a time when the poor people of the country have to pay extra for every drop of patent medicine they buy, when a poor country-woman cannot post a postcard without having to pay extra postage, when there are increased duties on boots and shoes and everything else, and when business is going to the dogs generally, one would think that the Minister of Inland Revenue would show some evidence of a desire to economize. The minister told us that some of this was represented by statutory increases of salaries to the officials, and when a man gets a statutory increase it is evidence of his ability to do his work satisfactorily, and there ought not to be any necessity for increasing the number of employees. It is true that the deputy minister of this department was a well-known lawyer in the city, without any qualification for a position in a department of this kind, and being appointed, and enjoying a high salary,
I suppose all the others in the department felt that they having some knowledge of the business of the department should get more pay. Another explanation may be that the ministers wanted to be kind to their new colleague in the Department of Inland Revenue, and there may have been reasons why they did not venture to suggest any interference with him, he being a man to be reckoned with. Perhaps the Minister of Finance and others of the ministers were afraid to discipline the new Minister of Inland Revenue, as he should have been disciplined, and hence they allowed him to increase the expenditure of his department. It might be all right if the country could afford it and if the Government were not piling on the taxes and bleeding the poor people white. If ever there was a time for economy surely it is now. Has the Minister of Inland Revenue increased his outside staff such as the preventive officers? If the minister has found that he has a preventive officer looking after the manufacture of illicit whisky in a district where illicit whisky has not been made for the last quarter of a century, is he still keeping that officer employed so as to give him some little reward for political services? There was a preventive officer in my country who had not instituted a prosecution for eight or nine years, and when the Conservatives came to power, there being nothing for him to do, they decided to dispense with his services. It was discovered that for the first few years he held office he had reported on two prosecutions and for the next nine years there was nothing to be done, and so the office was an honorary one, hut the officer being an old man they didn't discharge him. But he was finally discharged, and immediately after the change of government the then Minister of Inland Revenue employed another man, not-

withstanding that there was a report to the department that the services of such an officer were not required. In order to help him they made this new appointee food inspector and gave him $350 a year, but there was no food for him to inspect. I refer to an officer, in my own county, and I ask the minister now if there have been any prosecutions in that county since this officer was appointed. I do not believe that officer ever wrote a report because I know he has no duty to discharge. As a matter of fact, did this officer ever make a report to the minister?
What is his name?

Moses Delorey. He
is preventive officer and food inspector and he lives in a part of the county where there is no food exposed for sale. If he lived in a town or visited a town, there might be some reason for his going to the grocery stores and inspecting the food, but as a matter of fact he never did anything and never had anything to do. I am not saying anything against him personally because he is all right as a citizen of the community, and he is a loyal Conservative and he ought to have got a reward, but the Government ought to have rewarded him without doing anything so brazen as they have done and outraging public opinion and public morality. The people in that district, when they go to town have to pay an extra fare on the train; and they have to pay extra for everything they buy when they get to town, and probably they receive nothing more for the produce they have to sell, and in view of these conditions these supernumerary and unnecessary offices ought to be abolished.
I wish to refer to a matter that has not direct reference to this department. Some eight or nine immigration officers who were appointed for the province of Nova Scotia were given a three months' trip to the Old Country. Their salaries were $700 or $800 or $900. Separately the amounts are small, but collectively they are large. These agents have nothing to do. The one appointed for my county was a discharged railway sec-tionman. For some reason or another it was not convenient to replace him, and so he was made an immigration agent. There is on file in the department a report costing the country $800 or $900, and all the information contained in it is that up in the highlands of Scotland, whence this man's forefathers came, he met people who spoke Gaelic. We could get that information without paying $800 or $900 and with-[Mr. W. Chisholm.!
out sending a man all t'he way to the Old Country. The other officers who were appointed were men of the same class. With some two exceptions, they were illiterate and did not possess sufficient education to deliver public lectures describing the country whence they had come. I have nothing to say against them personally, but they were not fit for a position of that nature. They were appointed to these positions simply and solely as a reward for political service. My hon, friend the Minister of Inland Revenue has a number of the same class of men in his department. When he is trying to justify the increases in the inside service, he will see the necessity of lopping off these officials to whom I refer, who are neither ornamental nor useful.

I will give my best attention to the remarks of my hon. friend concerning Mr. Moses Delorey. The department has to have officers even in places where there is not much work to do, in order to prevent infractions of the law. The case of my hon. friend, of course, may be quite different.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: There is a report on file showing that this man's predecessor had nothing at all to do, and that the office could be abolished. In the face of that report my hon. friend is appointing another man and making him food inspector as well.

My hon. friend will admit that I am not responsible for his appointment as food inspector. I will inquire into the matter. The salaries in cases such as the one my hon. friend has mentioned are not much over $100 or at most $200. The reason that my hon. friend is giving, namely, the extra tax on the people, to induce me to be more economical in the management of my department, is the same reason which imposes more work upon my officers than they had in the past, as I am sure my hon. friend will realize.

The Tilbury Gas Company supplies gas to many places in my section, and I am sure the minister has received a number of communications complaining that the gas is not purified. The town of Brantford, I understand, is taking the matter up with my hon. friend. Last year Mr. Nantel, my hon. friend's predecessor, sent a man to that district to inspect the gas and to report. He reported that the gas contained sulphur, and that it was not fit to be supplied to the people without being purified. The company made arrangements

with the various corporations to purify the gas; but when it came to operating and it had got the gas into the people's houses for cooking, in some cases for lighting and in other cases for heating, the company immediately turned on the unpurified gas. I wrote to my hon. friend since he came into the department, pointing out that in the case of Woodstock, as soon as the cold weather started and an additional amount of gas was requiredrthe company turned on the unpurified gas, which was dangerous to the health of the people. We were placed in a peculiar position. We had an agreement with the company that they were to supply purified gas; but if we enforced the agreement and made them cut off the gas, the consequence would be that the people would have nothing with which to cook and some of them nothing with which to heat their houses. We were between the devil and the deep sea, and we had therefore to take the unpurified gas. I know a great deal about the matter, as I had to suffer from the effects of this unpurified gas. The department should be able to caucel the company's right to operate if it does not carry out its agreement, as T understand the law gives the department the right to force the company to supply purified gas. Hon. members could not stand the unpurified gas in this chamber for half an hour. Their heads would ache so much that they could not see, and unpurified gas is certainly not fit for use in houses. Has the minister taken any steps to force this company to supply purified gas to tne various municipalities?

I have received several letters in regard to the matter and some delegations have come to Ottawa. I have taken a great deal of interest in the question. My attention, however, was drawn to the fact that the particular section of the British North America Act mentioned as defining the scope of the powers of the Federal Government referred only to weights and measures, apparently leaving the quality of the gas to be dealt with by the provinces. My officers informed me that section 31 of the Gas Inspection Act, relating to the quality and purity of gas, was contested by some eminent lawyers as being beyond the powers of the federal authority. Therefore, I thought it best to refer the matter to the Department of Justice for its opinion as to the powers of my department, and I am expecting to receive their report at an early date.
Mr. NESBITT; Will you let me see the report when you receive it?
Yes.
Are there any preventive officers in the county of Inverness at present?.	.
I do not see that there is any.

The hon. minister in
replying to the hon. member for Antigonish justified the appointment of Mr. Delorey on the ground that his duty was to prevent the manufacture of whisky. And that is a good reason. There was a similar officer in Inverness, Mr. McDonald, who was dismissed, because evidently, the minister did not see very much for him to do. But if he will look up the history of his department he will find that, having regard to the past history of Antigonish and of Inverness, there will be more need for an officer in Inverness.

Because they made
whisky there?
Mr- CHISHOLM:	They used to charge
them with making some liquor there. I do not think they do it now. But if an officer were appointed it would make sure that they did not fall into the sins of former days. The hon. minister's predecessor dismissed Mr. McDonald because there was nothing for him- to do, and appointed the man in Antigonish; and there is nothing for him to do. The same reason that would justify the appointment in Antigonish would justify an appointment in Inverness. The man who was dismissed was a supporter of mine. But, as I am a believer in a measure that "To the victors belong the spoils" there may have been some justification for their action. But I understand that the difficulty about the appointment is that there are too many men who think that they ought to be appointed. I will try to influence my opponents to agree upon one man, and then I will suggest that he be appointed. Of course, he will be recommended by my defeated opponent, and then I hope he will be appointed.
With nothing to do-

No, nothing to do, but
that does not make any difference.

The dismissal may have been with a view to saving money, as in my own county. When we came into power in 1911, there was one preventive officer in Rimouski who had been appointed by the Liberals about ten years before, to do no-

thing. And when we came into power we found by the books that this man had actually been dismissed by the Liberal Government before they left office. They found that this man was doing so much nothing that they dismissed him themselves. We did not replace him because there was nothing for such an officer to do. My hon. friend from Antigonish should not be too much scandalized over the case he has referred to. If it is bad to appoint a man to do nothing, it must have been bad for his friends to appoint this man to do nothing and keep him in office for ten years.

If the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) did not get a man appointed in the Inland Revenue, he has been getting them appointed in the Railways and Canals Department all along the line from Moncton to Riviere du Loup. He is regarded with envy and admiration by other public men of that region, and with suspicion by his colleagues here because he is known as the greatest patronage hunter in the province of Quebec. We find the work of his hand as far down as Westmorland, and in western New Brunswick along the borders of the United States. His speech this evening is a real case of Satan rebuking sin. The minister stopped in his explanation at the translator. I wish he would go on with his explanation with regard to these other officers.
In the Second Division, Subdivision A, there is an additional officer. This is a new analyst required for the new laboratories opened in Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Halifax.
You are giving him $1,600. Has he been appointed?
This is to provide for his appointment.
You have no additions to the staff in the Methylated Spirits branch. You get along there without additional men?
Yes,

In the Electrical
branch, you need some assistance. Why?
